prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
explanation: Binary search halves the search space on each comparison, so the number of steps needed grows logarithmically with n — O(log n). This requires the array to already be sorted; sorting it first would cost O(n log n).
teachMePrompt: I just learned that binary search runs in O(log n) time. Teach me the full mental model behind that: how to set up and solve the recurrence relation that gets you from 'halve the problem each step' to O(log n), and how the same reasoning applies to other divide-and-conquer algorithms (merge sort, binary search trees, exponentiation by squaring). Don't just prove this one case — show me how to derive complexity for any halving algorithm.
doubleCheckPrompt: Is it accurate that binary search on a sorted array runs in O(log n) time complexity? Cite sources.

prompt: What does an HTTP 429 status code mean?
options: Too Many Requests — the client has been rate-limited
Forbidden — authentication succeeded but access is denied
explanation: 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given time window and is being rate-limited; the response often includes a Retry-After header. 500 is Internal Server Error, 403 is Forbidden, and 504 is Gateway Timeout.
teachMePrompt: I just learned what HTTP 429 means. Teach me the full mental model of HTTP status codes that signal backpressure or unavailability: how 429 (rate limited) differs from 503 (service unavailable) and 500 (server error), how the Retry-After header works across the codes that use it, and how a well-behaved client should react differently to each. Don't just define 429 in isolation — show me the whole family of codes it belongs to.
doubleCheckPrompt: Is it accurate that HTTP status code 429 means 'Too Many Requests' and signals client-side rate limiting? Cite sources.

prompt: What's the key difference between a process and a thread?
options: A thread has its own isolated memory space; a process shares memory with other processes
A process has its own memory space; threads within the same process share that memory space
There is no meaningful difference — the terms are interchangeable
Threads can run on multiple machines; processes cannot
explanation: A process gets its own isolated memory space from the OS. Threads are units of execution within a process, and all threads in that process share the same memory space — which makes inter-thread communication cheaper but introduces risks like race conditions that don't exist between separate processes.
teachMePrompt: I just learned the key difference between a process and a thread. Teach me the full mental model of OS-level concurrency: how memory isolation differs between processes and threads, why that isolation is what makes threads cheaper to spin up but more prone to race conditions, and how this same isolation tradeoff shows up in language-level choices (e.g. why CPU-bound work often reaches for multiprocessing instead of threading). Don't just define process vs thread — show me the underlying isolation model.
doubleCheckPrompt: Is it accurate that threads within the same process share the same memory space, while separate processes have isolated memory? Cite sources.
